Summary

This paper introduces a new task setting for product attribute mining in e-commerce: lightly supervised open-world attribute mining, where the goal is both to expand values for known seed attribute types and to discover previously unseen attribute types without explicitly naming them at inference time. To support this setting, the authors construct a new dataset, WoaM, spanning four Amazon product categories with seed attributes derived from sanitized product profiles plus light human curation, and a manually annotated test set. The proposed method, Amacer, is a pipeline with: (i) syntax-based candidate span generation using POS patterns, (ii) supervised contrastive representation learning from seed attributes, (iii) adaptive expansion of seed attributes plus DBSCAN clustering for remaining candidates, and (iv) two additional regularizers for open-world discovery: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence contrastive loss and an unsupervised latent-attribute/topic-modeling objective. Experiments show gains over closed-world tagging baselines and OA-Mine variants, with the strongest reported improvements on overall pseudo-F1 and on unseen attribute types.

Overall assessment

I think the paper tackles an important and practically motivated problem. The shift from zero-shot extraction of specified new attributes to automatic discovery of unnamed new attributes is meaningful, and the paper makes a credible case that this setting is underexplored and relevant for e-commerce. The dataset contribution also appears valuable, especially because it includes bullet-point descriptions rather than only titles. The method is sensible and reasonably well aligned with the weak-supervision setting. The empirical results are generally strong and the ablations are informative.

That said, I also have several concerns. The evaluation protocol is somewhat unconventional and may obscure what exactly is improving. The proposed “pseudo-F1” based on averaging clustering metrics is hard to interpret. The pipeline combines several design choices, and while the ablations help, some comparisons are not fully controlled. There are also questions about generality beyond four categories and beyond English/Amazon-style text. Finally, some methodological details remain underspecified, especially around clustering, thresholding, and the interaction between candidate generation quality and downstream gains.

Despite these concerns, I view the paper as a solid contribution with practical relevance.

Strengths

1. Important and realistic task formulation
The paper identifies a useful gap between closed-world extraction and zero-shot extraction with user-specified attributes. Automatically discovering new attribute types under limited supervision is a compelling setting for real product catalogs.

2. Valuable dataset contribution
WoaM seems meaningfully different from prior datasets in including longer product descriptions/bullet points and a substantial proportion of unseen attribute types and values. The seed-set construction process is also more thoughtful than naive distant supervision.

3. Method fits the problem setting
The use of syntax-based candidate generation, supervised contrastive learning from seeds, and clustering-based grouping is a natural fit for weak supervision. The adaptive expansion step is simple but effective.

4. Novel use of implicit signals
The self-supervised bullet-point heuristic and latent-attribute regularization are interesting additions. The latent-attribute component is especially appealing as a way to inject corpus-level structure for unseen attributes.

5. Strong empirical gains
The reported improvements over OA-Mine and other baselines are substantial. The decomposition by seed/new types and title/bullet points is useful and supports the paper’s claims.

6. Good qualitative analysis
The examples help illustrate both successes and failure modes, especially the tendency to absorb unseen attributes into semantically nearby seed types.

Weaknesses and concerns

1. Evaluation metric is hard to interpret
The main metric is a “pseudo-F1” derived from averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI as a pseudo-precision and combining that with recall. This is unconventional and not easy to reason about. Since Jaccard/ARI/NMI are clustering agreement metrics rather than precision measures, the resulting F1 does not have a standard interpretation. This makes it harder to assess practical significance and compare to future work.

I appreciate that the paper also reports the underlying clustering metrics and recall, but the headline result relies on this composite score. I would strongly prefer either:
- reporting the full set of metrics without collapsing them into pseudo-F1, or
- adding more standard extraction-oriented metrics for span detection and type assignment.

2. Candidate generation may dominate performance
The syntax-based candidate generation appears to be a major source of gains, perhaps as important as the representation learning innovations. The paper does compare segmentation-based and syntax-based variants, which is good, but the overall framing sometimes attributes gains to the full method when candidate generation itself is doing much of the work. Since span extraction remains weak overall (Table 5), it would help to more clearly separate:
- candidate recall/precision,
- clustering quality given gold spans,
- clustering quality given predicted spans.

The “Gold” column in Table 4 is a step in this direction, but more systematic analysis would strengthen the claims.

3. Limited scope of dataset and generalization
The dataset covers only four categories: Tea, Vitamin, Sofa, Phone Case. These are diverse to some extent, but still a small sample of e-commerce. It is unclear how well the POS-pattern approach and latent-attribute regularization would transfer to categories with very different language, noisier descriptions, or more technical specifications.

Similarly, the approach depends on English POS tagging and Amazon-style bullet points. The limitations section acknowledges this, but the paper’s broader claims about practical open-world attribute mining should be tempered.

4. Baseline comparisons are not fully satisfying
The strongest baseline, OA-Mine, is adapted in multiple ways (segmentation vs syntax candidates, different losses, etc.), but there is no broader comparison to more recent embedding/clustering or weakly supervised extraction methods beyond the cited task-specific systems. For example, stronger sentence/span embedding baselines, metric learning variants, or alternative clustering methods could be relevant.

Also, the closed-world tagging baselines are expected to underperform on open-world discovery, so their inclusion is useful mainly as a lower bound. The more meaningful comparison is against open-world methods under matched candidate sets and matched encoders.

5. Some methodological choices feel heuristic
Several components are reasonable but somewhat ad hoc:
- adaptive thresholding based on average intra-seed cosine distance times a scalar delta,
- using same-bullet-point spans as positives and different bullet points within the same product as negatives,
- choosing DBSCAN after adaptive expansion,
- selecting the number of latent attributes K as a hyperparameter.

These are not fatal issues, but the paper would benefit from more intuition or sensitivity analysis. For example, how stable is performance to K, delta, and the regularization weights? How often does the bullet-point heuristic create false positives because a bullet point mentions multiple unrelated attributes?

6. New attribute discovery is still modest
The paper rightly emphasizes the difficulty of the task, but “discovering values from 39% unseen attribute types” also indicates substantial room for improvement. This is not a flaw by itself, but it suggests the method is still far from robust open-world discovery. The paper should be careful not to overstate the maturity of the solution.

7. Annotation and evaluation details need more clarity
I would like more information on:
- inter-annotator agreement for the test set,
- how disagreements were resolved,
- whether annotators saw the seed ontology,
- how “reasonable attribute values” were defined operationally,
- how new attribute types were normalized across annotators.

Because open-world attribute typing is subjective, annotation consistency is especially important here.

Questions for the authors

1. How sensitive are the results to the number of latent attributes K and to the regularization weights λss and λun?
2. How much of the final gain comes from improved span extraction versus improved clustering/type discovery?
3. Did you measure inter-annotator agreement on span boundaries and attribute type assignments, especially for new types?
4. How often do the discovered clusters correspond to coherent but non-attribute concepts, rather than valid product attributes?
5. Why is the denominator in the supervised/self-supervised contrastive objectives written over negatives only, rather than all non-anchor examples as in standard supervised contrastive learning? Is this intentional, and did you compare formulations?
6. In adaptive expansion, what happens when a candidate is within threshold for multiple seed attributes?
7. How is DBSCAN configured across categories, and how sensitive are results to eps/minPts?
8. Could the latent-attribute model be used directly for clustering rather than only as a regularizer?

Suggestions for improvement

1. Improve evaluation clarity
Please foreground standard metrics and treat pseudo-F1 as secondary, or justify it more rigorously. A clearer decomposition into span detection, known-type assignment, and new-type discovery would help.

2. Add stronger controlled ablations
A table isolating each component under identical candidate spans would be useful:
- supervised contrastive only,
- + adaptive expansion,
- + self-supervised loss,
- + latent-attribute loss,
- + both regularizers.

3. Report annotation quality
Include inter-annotator agreement and more detail on the annotation protocol for new types.

4. Expand sensitivity analysis
Show robustness to K, delta, DBSCAN parameters, and seed-set size. Since the paper emphasizes light supervision, a curve over seed coverage would be especially valuable.

5. Clarify novelty relative to OA-Mine
The paper does improve substantially over OA-Mine, but the exact conceptual novelty should be stated more crisply: is the main novelty the task setting, the candidate generation, the adaptive expansion, the regularizers, or the combination?

6. Discuss failure modes more deeply
The qualitative section is helpful; it would be even stronger with a taxonomy of errors:
- missed spans,
- boundary errors,
- assigning new types to nearest seed types,
- splitting one attribute into multiple clusters,
- merging semantically distinct attributes.

Recommendation

Weak Accept

Rationale

The paper addresses a meaningful and underexplored problem, introduces a useful dataset, and proposes a practical method with strong empirical gains. The work is not flawless: the evaluation is somewhat unconventional, some comparisons could be more controlled, and the scope is limited. Still, I believe the task formulation and dataset are valuable contributions, and the method contains enough novelty and practical insight to merit acceptance.

Confidence

3/5

I am reasonably confident in my assessment based on the paper content, though some appendix details and implementation specifics are not fully visible here.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper introduces a new lightly supervised open-world product attribute mining setting for e-commerce, where the goal is both to expand known seed attribute types and to discover previously unseen attribute types without explicit type descriptions. The authors construct a new dataset, WoaM, spanning four Amazon product categories with curated seed attributes and human-annotated test data. They propose Amacer, a pipeline combining syntax-based candidate span generation, supervised contrastive learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion for known attributes, DBSCAN for residual clustering, and two forms of implicit supervision: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence objective and an unsupervised latent-attribute/topic-modeling objective. Experiments show substantial gains over closed-world tagging baselines and OA-Mine-style open-world baselines, especially on new attribute discovery.
strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored setting: open-world attribute mining with limited supervision, which is more realistic than closed-world extraction or zero-shot extraction requiring explicit target type names.

The dataset contribution appears meaningful: WoaM includes titles and bullet points, multiple categories, curated seed sets, and a substantial proportion of unseen attribute types and values in test data.
The proposed pipeline is well motivated and modular, with clear separation between candidate generation, representation learning, and grouping.
The syntax-oriented candidate generation is simple, scalable, and empirically stronger than segmentation-based alternatives in this setting.
The use of supervised contrastive learning for seed expansion is sensible and appears more effective than prior triplet/regression formulations.
The implicit supervision components for new attribute discovery are novel in this context and supported by ablations showing gains, especially on unseen attribute types.
Experimental comparisons are fairly broad, including closed-world, segmentation-based open-world, and syntax-based variants, plus ablations isolating major components.
The paper includes useful quantitative and qualitative analyses, including breakdowns by seed vs. new types and title vs. bullet-point text.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is somewhat unconventional: the main 'pseudo-F1' is derived from averaging clustering metrics (Jaccard, ARI, NMI) as a proxy for precision and combining that with recall. This metric is hard to interpret and may obscure practical extraction quality.

The method is a multi-stage pipeline with several heuristics and hyperparameters (POS patterns, adaptive thresholds, DBSCAN settings, latent attribute count), making it difficult to disentangle which components are essential and how robust the system is across settings.
The dataset covers only four product categories from Amazon, so claims about general open-world applicability may be somewhat limited.
Candidate span extraction remains a major bottleneck, with relatively low span-level exact F1, suggesting that downstream clustering improvements may be constrained by extraction quality.

The discovered 'new attributes' are evaluated only as unnamed clusters, which is reasonable for the task formulation but limits understanding of semantic usefulness and whether clusters correspond cleanly to coherent attribute types.
The latent attribute module is acknowledged to suffer from topic collapse/redundancy, and the paper does not deeply analyze stability or sensitivity of this component.

Some comparisons may not be fully balanced because the proposed syntax-based candidate generation itself provides a strong advantage over segmentation-based baselines, making it harder to isolate gains from representation learning alone.
soundness_issues: The overall methodology is plausible, but the main evaluation metric raises soundness concerns because averaging Jaccard/ARI/NMI into a pseudo-precision is ad hoc and not standard; conclusions based primarily on this score should be interpreted cautiously.

The adaptive expansion threshold is based on average intra-seed cosine distance scaled by a tuned factor, but there is limited theoretical or empirical justification for why this thresholding scheme should generalize across attributes with different variance structures.

The self-supervised heuristic assumes spans within the same bullet point are semantically related and spans across bullet points of the same product are less related; this is intuitive but noisy, and the paper provides limited direct validation of this assumption beyond aggregate gains.

The unsupervised latent-attribute objective is adapted from topic modeling over candidate spans, but because candidate spans themselves are noisy and extracted by heuristics, the latent distributions may partly model extraction artifacts rather than attributes; this risk is not thoroughly examined.

The seed set construction involves human curation and frequency-based sanitization from retailer-provided attributes, which improves quality but may bias the benchmark toward attributes that are easier to bootstrap from existing profiles.
Statistical significance is mentioned for the best score, but broader variance reporting across categories/seeds/runs is limited, making robustness harder to assess.
